title: Blind-Tasting Practice
quiz.0.question: Based on the notes for "Mystery Wine No. 1" (pale with an orange rim, rose and tar aromas, very high acidity and tannin), what is it most likely to be?
quiz.0.explanation: "Roses and tar" is Nebbiolo's most classic aroma signature; together with the pale colour, orange rim and very high acid/tannin structure, it fits Barolo perfectly.
quiz.1.question: Based on the notes for "Mystery Wine No. 2" (chamomile, white peach, round texture, bitter-almond finish), what is it most likely to be?
quiz.1.explanation: Chamomile and white peach, with a round texture and the classic bitter-almond finish, are the standard blind-tasting traits of Garganega (Soave). Pinot Grigio is lighter, and Verdicchio is higher in acid with fennel.
quiz.2.question: Based on the notes for "Mystery Wine No. 3" (fine bubbles, ripe yellow apple, intense toast/brioche, round texture), what is it most likely to be?
quiz.2.explanation: The intense toast rules out tank-method Prosecco and Asti. Ripe yellow apple and a round, creamy texture point to the warmer Franciacorta rather than the high-acid, cool Trento DOC.
quiz.3.question: In blind tasting, a red that is deep and opaque, with blackberry, volcanic ash and smoke, and extremely powerful, dense tannins is most likely which grape?
quiz.3.explanation: Deep colour, black fruit, smoky volcanic notes and extremely powerful tannins are the classic traits of Aglianico (e.g. Taurasi), the giant of the South.

slides.0.subtitle: Full SAT reasoning for three mystery wines
slides.1.title: The Three-Step Method for Practical Blind Deduction
slides.1.content:
This lesson gives full tasting notes for three "mystery wines" — a red, a white and a sparkling wine. Use the SAT system and deductive reasoning to work out the grape, area and quality level.

The Three-Step Method for Blind Deduction (practical version)

① Structure first
First assess acidity, tannin and body — these three narrow the field dramatically at once
E.g. high acid + high tannin → rule out Primitivo, Nero d'Avola → narrow to Nebbiolo/Sangiovese/Aglianico
② Find the aroma markers
Look for each grape's unique signature aroma: rose and tar? sour cherry and herbs? black fruit and smoke? bitter almond?
Finding the signature aroma = narrowing at once to 1-2 grapes
③ Conclusion
Structure + aroma + sight triple-confirmed → reach the most reasonable conclusion
Add a vintage estimate: rim colour + tannin texture + aroma type → estimate within ±5 years
slides.2.title: Mystery Wine No. 1: An Italian Red
slides.2.content:
Read the tasting notes below carefully and use SAT deduction to conclude on the grape, area and vintage range.

Tasting notes

  • Sight (S): pale garnet + a clear orange rim + high transparency
  • Aroma (A): 🔥 rose petal + 🔥 tar/asphalt, violet, liquorice, red cherry
  • Taste (T): very high acidity, very high but fine tannins, medium body, 14% ABV, a finish of 120+ seconds
  • Overall: elegant yet powerful, seemingly just entering its drinking window

The deduction

  • ① Structural filter: very high acid + very high tannin → rule out the South (Primitivo/Nero d'Avola)
  • ② Signature aromas: rose + tar → points strongly to Nebbiolo
  • ③ Visual confirmation: pale + orange rim → consistent with Nebbiolo's low anthocyanins
  • ④ Refinement: pronounced tar + a 120-second finish → Barolo > Barbaresco
  • Vintage estimate: orange rim + tar + already-fine tannins → 10-15 years
✅ Conclusion: Barolo DOCG (Nebbiolo), 10-15 years old, possibly a Riserva or single-vineyard MGA
slides.3.title: Mystery Wine No. 2: An Italian White
slides.3.content:
The second wine is an Italian white; analyse it with the same deductive method.

Tasting notes

  • Sight (S): pale gold + slight green glints + clear and bright
  • Aroma (A): 🔥 chamomile + white peach + almond blossom, green apple, minerality
  • Taste (T): medium acidity, no tannin, medium body, round texture, 🔥 a clear bitter-almond finish
  • Overall: delicate and round, very harmonious and balanced

The deduction

  • ① Structural filter: medium acidity + no tannin + white → the Italian white framework
  • ② Signature aromas: chamomile + white peach → the core signature of Garganega (Soave)
  • ③ Bitter almond: the most recognisable finish of Italian whites
  • ④ Elimination: Pinot Grigio is lighter; Verdicchio is higher in acid with fennel; Fiano has honey and hazelnut
  • Vintage estimate: green glints + fresh, no aged notes = young (1-3 years)
✅ Conclusion: Garganega (Soave DOC or Soave Classico), 1-3 years old
slides.4.title: Mystery Wine No. 3: An Italian Sparkling Wine
slides.4.content:
The third wine is an Italian sparkling wine; first judge the method, then identify the area.

Tasting notes

  • Sight (S): pale gold + fine, creamy bubbles + a persistent mousse
  • Aroma (A): 🔥 toast + brioche + biscuit (intense), ripe yellow apple, butter
  • Taste (T): high acidity, round creamy texture, no sweetness (Brut), a long finish
  • Overall: complex and elegant, with clear yeast-autolysis character

The deduction

  • ① Method: intense toast + fine bubbles → traditional method (not Charmat Prosecco)
  • ② Area filter: round + ripe yellow apple → Franciacorta (warmer Lombardy)
  • ③ Rule out Trento DOC: Trento is higher in acid with cooler minerality, not matching the roundness
  • ④ Rule out Champagne: Champagne's fruit leans more to green apple (cooler) with higher acidity
  • Age estimate: complex toast + roundness = long lees contact (possibly 30+ months)
✅ Conclusion: Franciacorta DOCG, traditional method, Brut
slides.5.title: Key Takeaways
slides.5.points.0: The three-step method: ① structure first → ② find the aroma markers → ③ conclusion; none can be skipped
slides.5.points.1: Wine 1 (Barolo): pale orange rim (S) + rose and tar (A) + very high acid and tannin, 120 s (T) = Nebbiolo, Barolo
slides.5.points.2: Wine 2 (Soave): chamomile and white peach (A) + bitter-almond finish (T) = Garganega, the most typical Italian white signature
slides.5.points.3: Wine 3 (Franciacorta): intense toast (A) = traditional method; round with ripe yellow apple = Franciacorta rather than Trento
slides.5.points.4: Identifying method: toast → traditional method; fresh fruit without toast → Charmat (Prosecco)
slides.5.points.5: The most common blind-tasting error: confirmation bias — once you form a hypothesis you look only for supporting evidence and ignore contradictions
slides.5.points.6: The right approach: collect all the SAT data first, conclude last, and actively look for contradictory features
slides.5.points.7: Integrating vintage clues: rim colour + aroma stage + tannin texture → estimate within ±5 years
slides.5.points.8: Blind tasting is deduction, not guessing — every conclusion needs at least 3 independent pieces of SAT evidence

slides.6.questions.4.question: What is the most dangerous psychological bias in blind tasting?
slides.6.questions.4.options.0: Relying too much on sight to rule out vintage clues
slides.6.questions.4.options.1: Confirmation bias: after forming a preconception, looking only for evidence that supports it
slides.6.questions.4.explanation: Confirmation bias is the most dangerous psychological trap in blind tasting: once you decide on a grape (e.g. Nebbiolo), you unconsciously look only for supporting evidence and ignore contradictory clues. One purpose of the SAT system is to force the taster to collect all the data before concluding.
